This opening unit defines governance and “good governance,” works through the standard characteristics of good governance, and concludes with how governance failure should be diagnosed.

blocks.text: .2 The Origin and Definition of Governance

segments.text: While the word “governance” has old linguistic roots, modern governance literature uses it specifically to study how authority and collective action operate not only through formal government but through a

— echoing the Governance Approach already introduced in the Public Administration chapter. Formally, governance refers to the processes and institutions through which authority is exercised, collective decisions are made and implemented, and public affairs are managed — with the important caution that different organizations and scholars define the term somewhat differently, so any formal definition quoted in an answer should be attributed to its specific source.

is a normative idea — a statement about desirable qualities institutions should have — rather than a single, universally agreed, precisely measured formula. The commonly cited characteristics, several of which overlap directly with the Core Values already introduced in the Public Administration chapter, are each worth understanding through their own precise logic:

items.text: Participation

— affected people and groups should have meaningful channels (direct or through legitimate representation) to express interests and influence public decisions. Its actual quality depends on genuine access, adequate information, inclusiveness across different groups, real ability to influence the eventual decision, and feedback about what happened to the input provided — participation without feedback or real influence is participation in form only.
Rule of law

— public authority should act strictly under law, rights should be protected, rules should be applied consistently to everyone, and lawful remedies should exist when authority is abused — developed in much greater depth as a specific governance indicator in Unit III below.
Transparency

— relevant public information, procedures, and the reasons behind decisions should be accessible enough to allow genuine understanding and scrutiny, subject only to legitimate legal limits (protecting genuine privacy, security, or confidentiality needs) — transparency is bounded, not absolute.
Responsiveness

— institutions should react to legitimate needs and complaints within a reasonable time, according to law and stated public priorities — importantly, this is not the same as unconditionally obeying every demand, since officials must also protect legality and the broader public interest (a point already made identically in the Public Administration chapter’s Bureaucratic Responsiveness topic).
Equity
— governance should avoid arbitrary exclusion, and should weigh fairness in access, treatment, and the distribution of public opportunities and services.
Effectiveness and efficiency

— effectiveness asks “did we achieve the intended result?”; efficiency asks “how much result did we obtain for the resources actually used?” A frequently tested point: an organization can be highly efficient while pursuing entirely the wrong objective, which is precisely why
both
criteria matter together, not either alone.
Accountability

— officials and institutions should be required to explain and justify their conduct to a body or to citizens capable of genuine review and, where appropriate, sanction — developed in much greater depth in Unit V below.
Strategic vision

— governance should not be confined to reacting to immediate pressures; institutions need a genuinely long-term view of public challenges, their own capabilities, demographic and technological change, and the longer-term consequences of today’s decisions.

segments.text: Governance failure should be diagnosed through

, not simply asserted as a label. Relevant evidence includes a demonstrated inability to provide core public services, persistent illegality, weak accountability mechanisms, genuine institutional breakdown, or a severe, evidenced loss of legitimacy or capacity. The syllabus’s important, frequently tested caution:
a single poor indicator on one specific governance dimension is not sufficient to establish total institutional failure

— genuine diagnosis requires converging evidence across capacity, legality, service delivery, accountability, and legitimacy together, and careless use of the label “failed state” or “failed institution” without this evidentiary basis is a common analytical error this unit specifically warns against.

items.text: Governance (the broader process) and government (the formal institution) are distinct — this distinction, introduced here, recurs throughout the subject and should be stated precisely whenever either term appears.

Good governance’s characteristics are not independent checkboxes; several trade off against each other in practice (e.g., broad participation can slow the speed valued by responsiveness) — a sophisticated answer notes these tensions rather than listing characteristics as though they were always mutually reinforcing.
Governance failure is a diagnosis requiring converging evidence across multiple dimensions, not a label applied on the strength of a single weak indicator.
